computer-vision.title: Field day: lawnmower search + live geolocation
computer-vision.summary: Ran the full search-to-geolocation loop outdoors for the first time — lawnmower coverage at 50 m AGL feeding real-time target coordinates to the flight controller.
computer-vision.imageAlt: Field testing of the onboard vision and search pipeline

body.text: Took Storm out to run the search pipeline start to finish instead of bench-testing the pieces separately. Flew the lawnmower pattern inside the search boundary at 50 m (164 ft) AGL — the altitude where the A8 Mini's 81° horizontal FOV gives roughly an 85.4 m swath per pass, wide enough to set line spacing with real overlap between legs instead of leaving gaps at the pattern edges.

body.alt: Field session validating search coverage and detection handoff
body.caption: Lawnmower pass over the search grid — first outdoor run of the full detection-to-reposition loop.

body.text: Every confirmed detection got run through the geolocation conversion live: pixel position to ground sample distance (about 2.01 cm/pixel at this altitude), then to a real-world offset using GPS position and fused heading, then to a geodetic target coordinate. The flight controller received that as a reposition command ahead of payload release.

body.heading: Notes from the field
items: Two passes needed a re-fly — direct sun glare over the tarp targets washed out contrast on the gimbal feed.
Reposition commands landed within expected tolerance on every run that didn't get re-flown.
Line spacing held overlap fine at 50 m; haven't pushed the pattern into gustier conditions yet.

body.text: Next up: repeat the same run in more wind than we saw today, and start actually logging detection-to-command latency instead of eyeballing it off the video feed.

computer-vision.title: Training run: YOLO detector on synthetic + real data
computer-vision.summary: Fine-tuned the YOLO detector for the two competition target classes; occlusion and orientation augmentation got cranked up after the last round undercounted partially-covered targets.
computer-vision.imageAlt: Vision model evaluation during field data collection

body.text: Spent this cycle on the detector instead of the airframe. Sticking with a YOLO single-stage model for the mannequin and tent classes — looked at DETR early on, but the gains transformer detectors report show up on datasets much larger than our synthetic-plus-real mix, so it wasn't worth the extra training complexity for us.

Training set is still mostly synthetic — target instances composited onto aerial backgrounds with randomized orientation, scale, lighting, and occlusion — topped up with real field imagery so the model sees actual camera noise and lighting the synthetic pipeline can't fake.

body.alt: Real aerial imagery used to supplement synthetic training data
body.caption: Real field captures added this round to cover debris clutter the synthetic set was missing.

body.heading: What changed this round
items: Cranked up occlusion augmentation after last month's model missed mannequins partially buried in debris — competition rules explicitly allow that, so it has to be covered.
Added full 0–360° orientation sampling instead of the narrower range we started with.
Real-image share of the training set is still small; want more field captures before the next retrain.

body.text: Next: pull more field photos from upcoming flight days and re-check validation on the occlusion-heavy cases specifically, not just aggregate mAP.

computer-vision.title: Camera decision: A8 Mini for mapping + detection
computer-vision.summary: Settled on the SIYI A8 Mini as our one camera for both risk mapping and target detection, running inference onboard instead of over the video link.
computer-vision.imageAlt: SkyXperts computer vision sub-team with the A8 Mini camera setup

body.text: Decided early that one gimbal camera has to cover both jobs — feeding the risk-map stitching pipeline and running target detection — with all inference happening onboard the Jetson. We looked at running detection on the ground station instead, but that ties the whole detection loop to the RF video link, which gets unreliable fast in a field with a dozen other teams' radios running.

Between the A8 Mini and a cheaper fixed action camera, the gimbal won out mainly for the global shutter and built-in stabilization. Keeping the optical axis close to nadir through turns and gust corrections matters a lot for how cleanly stitched mapping frames overlap — a shaky feed makes that job much harder downstream.

body.alt: Computer vision team working on the perception pipeline
body.caption: Bench-mounting the A8 Mini feed to the Jetson Orin Nano before the first onboard inference test.

body.heading: Open items
items: Need to confirm gimbal stabilization holds up in the wind speeds we expect on competition day, not just on calm bench tests.
Global shutter rules out most of the rolling-shutter smear we saw on the old action-cam footage during turns.

body.text: Next: get the A8 Mini feed running through the full onboard detection pipeline end to end, not just verified as a standalone feed.

computer-vision.title: Shaking out the vision scripts on the small test rig first
computer-vision.summary: Ran flight modes, detection scripts, and payload triggers on the smaller test platform before touching the real airframe — cheaper to crash.
computer-vision.imageAlt: Prototype multirotor used for early vision development

body.text: Before anything touches Storm, we run it on the small test platform first. This round covered flight mode switching, the early detection scripts, and the payload deployment trigger logic — all on hardware that's a lot cheaper to total than the competition airframe.

body.heading: Results
items: Flight mode transitions behaved as expected across the full test sequence.
Detection script ran without crashing for the whole test — accuracy wasn't the focus here, just making sure it doesn't fall over mid-flight.
Payload trigger fired correctly on command every time it was tested.

body.text: Nothing gets promoted to the full-scale build until it's held up on the test platform first — the point is to catch the dumb software bugs on the unit we don't mind breaking.
Next: start porting the validated scripts over to the Storm-specific hardware configuration and re-test against the real sensor stack.

control.title: Full mission dry run + failsafe trials
control.summary: Flew the complete mission end to end — takeoff, search, landing — then spent the rest of the day trying to break the failsafes on purpose.
control.imageAlt: Storm during autonomous field flight testing

body.text: First time we ran the complete mission profile back to back instead of testing each phase separately: autonomous takeoff, waypoint navigation out to the search area, the lawnmower search pattern, and landing. No manual intervention needed on any leg.

body.alt: Quadcopter hovering during outdoor flight testing
body.caption: Waypoint leg during the full-mission trial — wind was up more than we'd planned for.

body.text: Spent the second half of the day deliberately triggering failure conditions to check the response: killed telemetry, killed RC, forced a low-battery flag, and flew across the geofence boundary. Every trigger produced the expected response, no missed cases.

body.heading: Failsafe trial log
items: Telemetry loss → correct RTH trigger, every run.
RC loss → correct RTH trigger, every run.
Low battery flag → correct response, every run.
Geofence breach → flight termination triggered as expected.
Hardware kill switch on the RC transmitter disarmed the vehicle reliably on command, tested separately from the automated triggers.

body.text: Next: same test matrix again, but with the safety pilot and GCS operator swapping who calls each failsafe, so it isn't just one person's muscle memory being tested.

control.title: SITL first, then HITL, before anything flies
control.summary: Ran the mission software through Gazebo SITL function by function, then onto the real Pixhawk via HITL, before it was allowed anywhere near a real flight.

body.text: Two-stage validation before Storm's mission software touches actual hardware. First pass was SITL in Gazebo, tested piece by piece — searchAreaEntered(), waypoint navigation, the lawnmower search algorithm — each verified individually before running them together as one simulated mission.

Second pass was HITL: same mission code, but now talking to an actual Pixhawk 6C running the real PX4 firmware instead of a simulated flight stack. This is where we've caught driver-level issues before that SITL just can't see, since it isn't exercising the real hardware interfaces.

body.alt: Control sub-team integrating autonomy software
body.caption: Reviewing SITL mission logs before handing the same test matrix off to HITL.

body.heading: Results across both stages
items: All FSM state transitions fired correctly in SITL, no logic changes needed before moving to HITL.
HITL surfaced one MAVLink timing issue on a state transition that never showed up in simulation — traced and fixed before going further.
Flight termination triggers verified in both stages with no discrepancies.

body.text: Next: this code goes to physical flight trials now that both simulation stages are clean.

control.title: Locking the autonomy stack and failsafe timers
control.summary: Called it: Pixhawk 6C + PX4, M9N GPS, RFD900A telemetry, and hard numbers on the RTH and termination timers.
control.imageAlt: Storm airframe with avionics stack installed

body.text: Locked the core autonomy hardware and software stack today. Going with the Pixhawk 6C running PX4 — the deciding factor was native ROS 2 and MAVSDK support, which saves us from bolting on extra middleware just to get the autonomy layer talking to the flight controller.

GPS is the Holybro M9N — quad-constellation tracking at 25 Hz, which gets us under 2 m of position error. That's the accuracy margin we need to actually hold waypoint thresholds autonomously instead of hoping for the best.

body.alt: Storm quadrotor airframe
body.caption: Storm's avionics bay with the Pixhawk 6C stack installed.

body.heading: Failsafe timers, locked in
items: 15 seconds of comms loss → PX4 autonomously triggers RTH.
90 seconds → flight termination.
Safety pilot retains independent, single-action override to trigger either response at any time.
GCS operator has the same independent authority from the ground station.

body.text: These numbers aren't final-final — we'll stress-test them against real comms dropout behavior once RFD900A range testing wraps up.

control.title: Wiring PX4, ROS 2, and QGC into one pipeline
control.summary: Got the Jetson's ROS 2 autonomy layer actually talking to PX4 over MAVLink, with QGroundControl sitting on top for the operator.
control.imageAlt: Ground control station during mission rehearsal

body.text: This session was about getting the pieces to actually talk to each other instead of just working standalone. PX4 stays responsible for stabilization, state estimation, and waypoint execution; the Jetson Orin Nano runs the ROS 2 autonomy layer on top, subscribing to vehicle state and publishing mission commands back down over MAVLink.

body.alt: Field operations with ground control monitoring
body.caption: Ground station monitoring during the first end-to-end pipeline test.

body.text: QGroundControl is what the GCS operator actually watches during a run — flight boundary, vehicle position, ground speed, AGL altitude, all live. It's also the only interface we're using for mission upload, so it needs to hold up for the full 45-minute competition window, not just a quick test flight.

body.heading: First integration test notes
items: MAVLink bridge held a stable connection for the full test duration, no dropped commands.
One mission upload needed a retry — QGC timed out on a slow serial handshake, not repeatable so far.
ROS 2 autonomy commands reached the flight controller with no observed lag.

body.text: Next: keep an eye on that upload timeout if it shows up again, and start running longer sessions to make sure nothing degrades over a full 45-minute window.

electrical.title: Two kinds of failure, one checklist
electrical.summary: Wrote the power system lessons into an actual pre-power-on checklist — and started logging current on every flight, so the next thermal failure comes with data attached.
electrical.imageAlt: Ground station monitoring power telemetry during a mission rehearsal

body.text: Looking back at the power system over the past year, we managed to hit two completely different categories of failure, and it took us longer than it should have to notice they were different problems.

The first was a sizing problem. Motors, pack, PDB, power module — they all answer to the same rule, which is that you design against worst-case sustained load with real margin instead of typical load with none. We were disciplined about that with the battery and then quietly failed to apply it to the module measuring the battery.

The second was a handling problem, and no amount of component selection would have touched it. Going digital fixed an accuracy problem. Going to higher continuous ratings fixed a thermal problem. Neither one stops a terminal from touching another terminal during a wiring session.

body.alt: Ground control station during a mission rehearsal
body.caption: Voltage and current now get logged on every flight instead of just watched on the ground station.

body.heading: What's written down now, instead of assumed
items: Every current-carrying component gets sized against the measured worst-case sustained draw, and the number it was compared against gets recorded in the same document as the part number.
Continuous ratings drive the decision. Burst ratings are a footnote.
Voltage and current telemetry gets logged on every flight. We couldn't explain the June regulator failure because we had no data from the moment it happened, and we're not doing that twice.
Terminals insulated, polarity metered, one polarity at a time, disconnect procedure rehearsed — before an integration session starts, not partway through it.
Bench-test the real power path, ESC and servo included, before anything flies. That one we learned back in December on the payload servo, and it keeps being true.

body.text: None of this is a clever engineering insight. It's mostly the stuff everyone already nods along to, which is exactly why it had to become procedure instead of good intentions.
Next: fly the timed endurance test we've been putting off since March, now that the telemetry it depends on is worth reading.

electrical.title: Shorted a pack during re-integration
electrical.summary: A positive and a negative terminal touched while the new power module was going back in. The pack measured about 0.7 mV afterward — it was finished.
electrical.imageAlt: Electrical team working on power module integration

body.text: This one wasn't a design problem. It was a wiring-work problem. While we were re-integrating the new power module, a positive terminal and a negative terminal made contact and shorted.

A dead short across a pack is limited by almost nothing except the pack's own internal resistance, and on a 28 Ah lithium pack there isn't much of that. The battery stopped working on the spot. We measured it afterward at roughly 0.7 mV, which on something with a 22.2 V nominal is just zero with extra decimal places.

body.alt: Electrical sub-team during power module integration
body.caption: Integration work on the power module bay — insulated terminals are a written rule here now, not a habit.

body.text: Whether the short drove the cells into a damaging over-discharge or tripped an internal protection circuit into a latched near-zero state, we genuinely can't say. Telling those two apart means opening the pack up, and we don't have that data. Either way it was out of service.

The part that bothers us is that this happened during routine re-integration, on hardware we'd already handled carefully once. Nobody was rushing or doing anything unusual. That's generally how this category of failure goes — it isn't the task that feels dangerous that gets you.

body.heading: Changed the same day
items: Exposed pads and bus bars get heat-shrink or tape before integration work starts, not after something has already touched.
One polarity connected at a time wherever the harness allows it.
Polarity checked with a multimeter on any new or modified harness before its first connection.
A connected battery means live rails, no exceptions — nobody reaches past a powered board with a metal tool because it looks fine.
Disconnect procedure written down and rehearsed, so a fault gets an immediate response instead of three people working out whose job it is.

body.text: Next: replace the pack, finish re-integration under the new handling rules, and get back to flight testing.

electrical.title: Power architecture locked: one battery, two regulated rails
electrical.summary: Finalized how power gets from the single 6S battery out to everything else — PM08-CAN for avionics, PDB for propulsion and the Jetson buck.
electrical.imageAlt: Electrical team wiring Storm power distribution

body.text: Locked the full power distribution architecture this week, now that the replacement hardware has been through bench testing. Everything runs off a single MAD 6S 28 Ah solid-state lithium-ion pack (140 A continuous / 280 A max), routed through a PM08-CAN 14S 200 A power module and a 300 A side-entry PDB.

body.alt: Electrical sub-team working on avionics integration
body.caption: Harness routing from the PM08-CAN and PDB during power architecture bring-up.

body.heading: Rail assignments
items: PM08-CAN → 5.1 V rail → Pixhawk 6C, which in turn powers the RFD900A telemetry radio, RC receiver, Holybro M9N GPS, and the MG995 servo.
PDB → 22.2 V rail → all four ESCs and the SIYI A8 Mini gimbal.
PDB → 300 W buck converter → 18 V → Jetson Orin Nano.

body.text: Kept avionics and propulsion on physically separate rails on purpose, so a propulsion-side current spike doesn't have a path to brown out the flight controller or companion computer.
Next: re-integrate the whole thing into the airframe now that each rail has been verified under simultaneous load on the bench.

electrical.title: New distribution hardware: 300 A PDB and a digital power module
electrical.summary: Replaced the PM07 with a PM08-CAN and a 300 A side-entry PDB — more than double the continuous headroom, plus telemetry that doesn't depend on us calibrating it correctly.
electrical.imageAlt: Storm avionics bay during power module replacement

body.text: Reselected the whole distribution and sensing layer, this time against the 246 A worst case we measured in May rather than against what hover looks like. A 300 A side-entry power distribution board takes the propulsion side. A PM08-CAN, rated 200 A continuous, handles sensing and the regulated rail.

Continuous rating is the number that decided this. Burst ratings are real and they're useful, but a burst rating tells you about a spike during an aggressive maneuver — it says nothing about whether a board survives forty minutes of mission. Going from 90 A continuous to 200 A on the sensing path more than doubles the thermal headroom, and the PDB's heavy copper keeps resistive losses, and the heat they turn into, down on the distribution side.

body.alt: Storm airframe with the new power distribution hardware installed
body.caption: New PDB and PM08-CAN going into the avionics bay.

body.text: The other half of the fix is that the PM08-CAN reports over DroneCAN instead of an analog line. It sends pre-scaled digital telemetry, calibrated at the factory, with the current sensor galvanically isolated from the motor rail. That deletes the scaling constants we got wrong in February — not by us getting better at calibrating them, but by leaving nothing to calibrate.

It isn't a free upgrade. It costs more, and it puts a CAN bus in the critical path for battery telemetry, which is a dependency we didn't have before. We think that's a good trade for numbers we're willing to fly failsafes off, but it is a trade rather than a straight improvement.

body.heading: Checked after the swap
items: Reported pack voltage and current against a handheld meter — they agree out of the box, no constants touched.
Battery percentage tracked sensibly across a full discharge instead of wandering.
Re-counted every load hanging off the regulated rail, transient ones like the release servo included, so the buck converter isn't quietly carrying something we forgot about.
Ran the rail under simultaneous load on the bench before any of it went back into the airframe.
The module is 14S-rated and we're running 6S, so a chunk of that spec is headroom we'll never use.

body.text: Next: re-integrate into the airframe and write the rail assignments down properly, so this configuration is documented instead of remembered.

electrical.title: Smoke off the buck regulator after our first full mission
electrical.summary: Flew the complete mission, landed clean, then watched smoke come off the PM07's regulator on the ground. Battery came off immediately and nothing else was damaged.
electrical.imageAlt: Storm during the full mission flight test

body.text: The aircraft was assembled, so we flew the whole mission profile. The flight was uneventful. A little after landing, pack still connected, we saw smoke coming off the buck regulator on the PM07.

Battery came off straight away. We got lucky: the regulator was the only thing that died, and nothing else on that rail — flight controller, GPS, radios, Jetson — showed any damage when we went over it afterward.

body.alt: Quadcopter in flight during the full mission profile test
body.caption: The flight itself was fine. The failure showed up on the ground, minutes after landing.

body.text: The honest version of the root cause is that we have a strong hypothesis and no confirmation. A buck converter dumps heat into its switching element and inductor, the PM07's board is rated for 90 A continuous, and there's no forced airflow over it. Hover sits somewhere in the low 40s including avionics, comfortably inside that rating, which explains why bench runs and short hops never showed a problem. A full mission with real climbs and gust corrections is a different duty cycle entirely.

What we can't tell you is what the current actually was when it let go, because we weren't logging it. That's on us, and it irritates more than the dead part does — a cheap regulator failed and we have no number to explain it with.

body.heading: What we already knew and didn't put together
items: We measured 61.5 A per motor at full throttle on May 5, a month before this flight. 246 A across four motors was written down and agreed on.
The PM07's 90 A continuous rating was also written down — in a different document, on a different day.
Nobody put those two numbers next to each other until there was smoke in the air.

body.text: That's the mistake worth naming properly. We sized the battery against worst-case sustained load with margin, then picked the power module against roughly what we expected on a normal flight. Same aircraft, two different standards, and only one of them was any good.
Next: reselect the distribution and sensing hardware against the 246 A figure with proper margin, and fix February's telemetry problem in the same pass.

electrical.title: Bench test: pushing the motors to full throttle to size the ESCs
electrical.summary: Ran each motor to full throttle on the bench to confirm the 80 A ESCs actually have margin — measured 61.5 A max draw per motor.
electrical.imageAlt: Thrust versus current curve at takeoff operating point

body.text: Put each Avenger 4215 V5 on the bench and ran it up to full throttle to get a real current number instead of trusting the datasheet estimate. Measured 61.5 A per motor at full throttle — that's the number we sized the ESCs against.

body.alt: Spline fit of thrust versus current at takeoff
body.caption: Spline fit of the bench data — takeoff operating point at 2616 gf per motor, ~14.54 A estimated draw.

body.text: Paired each motor with a Hobbywing Skywalker 80 A V2 ESC, which puts us at roughly 30% current headroom above the worst-case measured draw. Not massive margin, but enough that we're not living right at the ESC's rated limit during takeoff.

body.heading: Wiring sized against worst case, not typical case
items: Battery output leads: 10 AWG, rated for simultaneous full-throttle draw across all four motors (246 A).
PM08-CAN leads: 8 AWG, same worst-case basis.
That worst-case draw is brief — full-throttle-on-all-four is a takeoff-only condition, not sustained — but we sized for it anyway.

body.text: Next: re-run this at sustained full throttle for longer than a single spike, since ESC thermal limits are usually a duration problem, not an instantaneous one.

electrical.title: Endurance math: 29.93 minutes, on paper
electrical.summary: Built the full endurance model combining avionics draw with phase-specific motor currents — comes out to just under 30 minutes on the 28 Ah pack.
electrical.imageAlt: Thrust versus current curve at cruise operating point

body.text: Put together the endurance model this week instead of just eyeballing flight time. Avionics alone draw a steady 35.4 W — Pixhawk 6C, A8 Mini, M9N GPS, RFD900A, RadioMaster ER8, and the Jetson Orin Nano combined — which works out to about 1.59 A off the 22.2 V nominal pack voltage.

body.alt: Spline fit at cruise operating point
body.caption: Cruise operating point from the spline fit — 1962 gf per motor, ~10.12 A estimated draw.

body.alt: Spline fit at landing operating point
body.caption: Landing operating point — 1308 gf per motor, ~5.87 A estimated draw.

body.text: Combined the per-motor current at takeoff, cruise, and landing with that constant avionics draw, and budgeted only 80% of the pack's rated 28 Ah as usable — didn't want to plan a mission around the last 20% of a lithium pack. Comes out to roughly 29.93 minutes of flight time.

body.heading: Caveats on this number
items: This is a bench-derived model, not a measured flight time — haven't run a timed endurance flight to check it against yet.
Doesn't account for wind loading, which will eat into cruise current on a real mission.
The 80% usable-capacity assumption is conservative on purpose; the real number is probably a bit higher.

body.text: Next: fly a timed endurance test in calm conditions and see how close the real number lands to 29.93 minutes.

electrical.title: The PM07's readings didn't match the meter
electrical.summary: First power module pick was Holybro's PM07. Once it was integrated, the voltage and current it reported disagreed with what we measured — analog sensing needs a calibration we hadn't done.
electrical.imageAlt: Bench setup verifying power module telemetry against a meter

body.text: Our first pick for the sensing and distribution layer was Holybro's PM07. It's a sensible default: analog voltage and current sensing, integrated 5 V regulator, cheap enough that nobody spends a design review arguing about it.
Once it was integrated, the numbers coming back were wrong. Pack voltage and current both disagreed with a handheld meter, and not by a tidy fixed offset we could shrug off as a display quirk.

body.alt: Bench setup for checking reported current against a reference meter
body.caption: Checking reported current and voltage against a meter on the bench.

body.text: That's the catch with analog sensing. The module puts out a voltage proportional to current and pack voltage, and the autopilot converts that back into amps and volts using scaling constants — volts per amp, amps per volt. Those ship with defaults, and a default is an educated guess about a generic board, not a calibration of our board with our harness. They're meant to be checked against a meter and ideally a power analyzer. We hadn't done it.

The other thing about shunt and Hall-effect sensing is that it's least trustworthy at low current. Below a few amps the reading is about as much noise as signal, and our avionics rail lives right in that range.

body.heading: Why this is worse than a cosmetic bug
items: Remaining capacity is computed from the current reading. Bad current in, bad state of charge out.
The low-battery failsafe fires off that estimate, so a wrong number moves return-to-launch earlier or later than we designed for.
We sized the pack around a known margin specifically so we'd know where we stood mid-mission. Uncalibrated telemetry hands that back.

body.text: We could have calibrated it and moved on — that's the normal fix, and we did start down that road. In parallel we started asking a different question, which was whether we wanted a hand-maintained calibration in the loop at all.
Next: run dedicated thrust and current tests on the motors with a power analyzer, so the propulsion numbers stand on their own instead of resting on whether we trust this module.

electrical.title: Sizing the pack, then checking the part that actually bites
electrical.summary: Sized the battery off combined propulsion and avionics draw with a 20% margin, then checked the C-rating separately — average current isn't what makes a pack sag.
electrical.imageAlt: Cruise operating point on the thrust versus current curve

body.text: Battery sizing came down to one relationship and then a second check that's easy to skip. The first one: required capacity is total average current draw times mission duration, plus margin, divided by the fraction of the pack we're actually willing to use.

We put 20% on top of that. The margin isn't decoration. It covers wind we can't predict, maneuvering more aggressive than a planning spreadsheet assumes, capacity that goes missing in cold weather, and the plain fact that a pack's usable capacity is a fair bit less than its rated capacity if you'd rather not deep-discharge cells on every flight.

body.alt: Spline fit of thrust versus current at the cruise operating point
body.caption: Cruise-point current — the figure the average-draw half of the sizing math leans on.

body.text: The second check is the C-rating. Capacity times C gives maximum continuous discharge, and that has to clear the highest current we expect in a full-throttle climb, not the mission average. A pack can be sized correctly for average draw and still sag badly under peak load if its C-rating is short, and sag is its own problem: the voltage drops exactly when we're asking for the most thrust, so it eats the margin we thought we had.
That's how we landed on the MAD 6S 28 Ah solid-state pack — 140 A continuous, 280 A max, which left room above the peak we were projecting at the time.

body.heading: What we weren't claiming yet
items: That projected peak was still a paper number in January. The measured one didn't arrive until we got motors onto a test stand.
We budgeted 80% of rated capacity as usable, which is conservative on purpose and probably leaves something on the table.
Mission duration is an assumption here, not a result — there's no timed endurance flight behind it.

body.text: Next: build a proper endurance model out of phase-by-phase current instead of one flat average, since takeoff, cruise, and landing don't draw anything like the same.

electrical.title: Chasing down payload release failures that weren't real
electrical.summary: 47 out of 50 bench releases succeeded — the other 3 turned out to be a test-setup mistake, not a mechanism problem.

body.text: Ran 50 bench trials of the payload release mechanism and got 47 clean releases. Spent longer than expected chasing down the other 3 failures before realizing it wasn't the mechanism at all.

The servo was being bench-tested in isolation without an ESC in the loop. Turns out the servo pulls its power through the ESC's BEC output rather than an independent supply, so testing it standalone with no ESC connected produced power starvation that looked exactly like a mechanical failure.

body.heading: What we got wrong, and the fix
items: Root cause: servo power path runs through the ESC BEC, not a dedicated rail — missed that in the original bench setup.
Fix: added the ESC into every servo bench test from now on, matching the actual airframe wiring.
Re-ran the 3 failed trials with the ESC connected — all 3 released cleanly.

body.text: Lesson logged for the whole team: any servo-driven subsystem gets bench-tested with its real power path from now on, not powered on its own for convenience.

electrical.title: Budgeting the small rail: what the avionics actually pull
electrical.summary: Built the avionics power budget line by line with the software sub-team — about 35 W on paper, and the entire reason it gets a rail of its own.
electrical.imageAlt: Sub-teams reviewing the onboard avionics package together

body.text: Spent this cycle on the least interesting number in the whole build. The software sub-team was settling which onboard avionics package to run, so we sat in on that and put together a line-by-line power budget alongside it: Pixhawk 6C, Holybro M9N GPS, RFD900A telemetry, the RadioMaster ER8 receiver, the SIYI A8 Mini, and the Jetson Orin Nano.

Each line came off a datasheet at the duty cycle we expect to run it at, then got added up. First pass came out somewhere around 35 W. On an aircraft where four motors can pull a couple hundred amps between them, that's a rounding error.

body.alt: Cross-sub-team review session
body.caption: Sitting in with the software sub-team while the avionics package got settled.

body.text: It still gets its own regulated rail, and that's not caution for its own sake. A dip on the propulsion rail costs thrust for a moment. A dip on this rail can reset the flight controller in the air. Two different failures with very different consequences, so they don't share a supply.

body.heading: Caveats we wrote down at the time
items: These are datasheet numbers, not measured ones. The Jetson in particular will draw whatever the vision workload asks of it, and "typical" on a spec sheet is not a promise.
An average figure hides transient loads — servo actuation, radio transmit bursts — and those are the ones that stress a regulator.
Plan is to re-measure the whole rail on the bench once there's real hardware to put a clamp around.

body.text: Next: take this budget and the propulsion current numbers into battery sizing, which is where the two finally get added together.

electrical.title: The power system starts with a number we didn't pick
electrical.summary: Mechanical handed over an all-up weight estimate and we turned it into a per-motor thrust requirement — 2:1 thrust-to-weight as the floor, not the goal.
electrical.imageAlt: Electrical team working through early power system sizing

body.text: The electrical side of this build didn't start with a battery or a motor. It started with a number from the mechanical team: an estimated all-up weight of just under 7 kg with payload. Every choice downstream — motors, ESCs, pack, distribution hardware — traces back to that figure, which is a slightly uncomfortable place to begin, because early mass estimates move and ours did.

We're treating 2:1 thrust-to-weight as a floor. It's a common starting point for a multirotor that has to stay maneuverable, and the logic is simple enough: we want authority left over to fight a gust and recover attitude while still climbing, not just barely enough to hold a hover. At that weight, 2:1 means roughly 14 kgf of total static thrust, so about 3.5 kgf per motor on a quad.

body.alt: Electrical sub-team during early sizing work
body.caption: Early power system sizing, well before any hardware got ordered.

body.text: The 2:1 figure isn't a law, though it gets quoted like one. The right margin depends on the mission, the wind we expect, and how much control authority the autopilot needs to hold a waypoint in gusts. It gets validated against the actual motor, prop, and ESC combination at the pack voltage we'll really be flying, not accepted from a rule of thumb.

body.heading: What this one number ends up deciding
items: Motor and prop pairing, checked against manufacturer thrust curves at expected pack voltage rather than the nominal figure on the front of the spec sheet.
Peak current per motor, which sets the ESC rating.
Four times that peak, which sets the battery leads, the distribution hardware, and the C-rating the pack has to meet.
None of it is final until it's been on a test stand and measured.

body.text: Next: hand the thrust requirement to the propulsion trade study, and start building the avionics power budget in parallel, since the same pack has to carry both.

mechanical.title: Storm is airframe-complete
mechanical.summary: Airframe build is done — 5 kg quadrotor-X, 4.09:1 thrust-to-weight, and it folds down small enough to fit a personal-item bag.

body.text: Called the airframe build complete this week. Storm comes in at 5 kg without payload — a from-scratch quadrotor-X built specifically around the five SUAS 2026 mission tasks instead of adapting an off-the-shelf frame.

body.alt: Storm quadrotor on display
body.caption: Storm, fully assembled and ready for the next round of flight testing.

body.heading: Where the numbers landed
items: Four Avenger 4215 V5 motors, each rated for 6902 g static thrust, against a 6750 g all-up weight including payload — 4.09:1 max thrust-to-weight.
Folded footprint: 18 × 14 × 8 in, small enough to travel in a personal-item bag for the Design for Rapid Response task.
That thrust margin is there for gust rejection in wind up to 14 mph and reserve authority during payload drop maneuvers, not just for looking good on paper.

body.text: Airframe done just means it's ready for the next round of flight testing — haven't pushed it anywhere near that 14 mph gust number in real conditions yet.

mechanical.title: Landing gear failed the drop test — here's what we changed
mechanical.summary: First landing gear design cracked on a 2 m drop test. Redesigned it, dropped it again, and it held.

body.text: Ran the landing gear through a 2 m drop test and it failed on impact. Not the outcome we wanted, but exactly why we test before committing to a design.

body.alt: Mechanical sub-team reviewing airframe components
body.caption: Inspecting the failed landing gear before starting the redesign.

body.text: Reworked the leg geometry and rebuilt it, then dropped it from the same 2 m height again. This time it held with no visible damage.

body.heading: Same day, motor mount test
items: Ran all four motors at full throttle for a sustained 1-minute ground test.
No deformation, no loosened fasteners, no mount failure observed afterward.
Full FEA factor-of-safety analysis is still running in parallel — the physical test passing doesn't mean we skip that step.

body.text: Next: repeat the landing gear drop test from a greater height to find where the new design actually fails, instead of just confirming it clears the minimum bar.

mechanical.title: Locking the frame material and mass budget
mechanical.summary: Went with sandwich composite plates after tracking mass at the component level — battery and payload alone are 39% of AUW.
mechanical.imageAlt: Carbon fiber frame construction on Storm

body.text: Tracked mass line by line at the component level this cycle instead of just weighing finished assemblies, and it paid off — the battery and payload together account for roughly 39% of all-up weight. That's a big enough chunk that it drove material decisions everywhere else on the frame.

Went with sandwich composite construction for the structural plates: a 600 g fiberglass core between two multi-directional carbon fiber face layers. Gets close to solid carbon fiber stiffness-to-weight without the full material cost, which matters when the battery and payload are already eating that much of the budget.

body.alt: Carbon fiber frame construction on Storm
body.caption: Sandwich composite plates and carbon fiber arms integrated into the airframe.

body.heading: Manufacturing notes
items: Built a full-scale mockup before committing to composite manufacturing, just to catch dimension and fitment issues cheaply.
Frame plates are cut by an outsourced composites shop using vacuum bagging, then CNC-finished to final geometry.
Arms are carbon fiber for the same stiffness-to-weight reasoning as the plates.

body.text: Next: lock the mockup-validated dimensions with the composites shop and start on the actual production plates.

mechanical.title: Two release mechanisms, one drop test day
mechanical.summary: Trap door for the flare, bracket latch for the water bottle — first drop tests landed within 30–75 ft of target from 10 m.

body.text: Built two separate release mechanisms since the two payloads don't behave the same way: a servo-actuated trap door for the flare, and a servo-driven bracket latch for the water bottle. Looked at a winch-based delivery system for both early on but dropped it — extra weight and slower deployment time than a 45-minute mission window can really afford.

body.alt: Cross-sub-team review before integration milestone
body.caption: Preliminary drop test — impact points landed within 30–75 ft of target from 10 m altitude.

body.heading: First drop test results
items: All test drops released cleanly from both mechanisms.
Impact points landed within 30 to 75 ft of the target from a 10 m drop altitude — usable, but a wider spread than we want for competition scoring.
Custom non-structural mounts (landing gear connectors, GPS mount, payload housing, camera bracket) are all FDM-printed in PLA+, holding up fine through this round of testing.

body.text: 30–75 ft is too wide a spread to call this done. Next iteration needs tighter release timing or a better drop-point calculation, not just repeated tests of the same setup.

mechanical.title: Motor and prop trade study — three options down to one
mechanical.summary: Bench-compared three motor options and two props before settling on the Avenger 4215 V5 and the 15558 folding tri-blade.

body.text: Bench-tested three motor candidates before picking one. The AT4125 Long Shaft pulled 72 A at full throttle versus 61.5 A for the Avenger 4215 V5 — worse on current draw and more expensive, an easy cut. The T-Motor U7 V2.0 got ruled out too, mostly on cost and because it doesn't fold down well for transport.

Prop comparison came down to two folding tri-blades. The 1248 only made 6676 g of thrust per motor at 3.21 g/W, while the 15558 hit 6902 g at 3.79 g/W — more thrust and meaningfully better efficiency, so that one was the clear pick.

body.alt: Spline fit at cruise operating point
body.caption: Thrust-current curves from the motor and prop bench comparison.

body.heading: Other changes made off the back of this round
items: Motor arms switched from aluminum to carbon fiber for better strength-to-weight over the previous platform.
Landing gear stance widened for better lateral stability landing in gusty conditions.

body.text: Next: get the selected motor/prop combo mounted on the actual airframe and re-run the thrust-current bench test in that configuration, not just on the test stand.
